header:
Date: 2027-11-02
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Raj Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Khan (Velorum Head of ML), Emma Li (Platform Eng), James Park (CTO)
summary: Initial POC scoping to decompose latency SLOs (TTFT vs TPOT), align on business risk, define measurement plan and bench roadmap. Customer cares about 99th pct tail under burst, and unit cost; wants hybrid acceptance criteria that includes both TTFT p95 and TPOT p99 for different call types. Agreed to run controlled benchmarks in Redwood sandbox with sampled production traces.
topics: TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs and definitions
Candidate SLO targets (p95/p99) and acceptance criteria
Measurement plan: sampling, synthetic vs replayed traffic
Benchmark orchestration, infra constraints and data handling
Timeline and responsibilities for the 3-week pilot
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, quick roll call then we'll jump in. I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Raj is our SE.
[00:12] Samir (Velorum): Hey Maya, thanks. Samir here, head of ML at Velorum. Emma and James are with me.
[00:18] Emma (Velorum): Hi all.
[00:20] James (Velorum CTO): Hey, good to be here.
[00:22] Raj (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. Agenda is to align on SLO decomposition TTFT versus TPOT, define targets, and sketch a measurement plan for the POC.
[00:30] Samir: Yep that's right. To start — quick context: we run a mix of short assistant-style prompts and longer completion workflows for analytics. Latency is visible to customers on the UI for the assistant flows, and for batch jobs cost matters more.
[00:44] Maya: Perfect. Can you share rough traffic shape and token counts? I know you pasted some numbers in the form but a couple highlights will help.
[00:52] Samir: Sure. Most interactive AI calls are 8 to 40 tokens in prompt, responses 20 to 150 tokens. 70% of calls are interactive low-latency; 30% are heavier generation tasks. Peak qps currently about 120 across region us-east-1, sustained 40 qps. Peaks are short bursts 60-90s.
[01:14] Emma: We also have multi-tenant routing, some customers are on dedicated plans; any PII is stripped before logs.
[01:21] Raj: Understood. So preliminary: for interactive flows we generally recommend TTFT p95 targets because user perceived latency is dominated by first token. For completions, TPOT (per-token throughput) or total time per request is more important. But we want to make sure TPOT tail at p99 doesn't blow up your costs.
[01:39] Samir: Quick question — folks on our infra care about p99 across the board, they're skeptical of ignoring tails. Can we do both?
[01:46] Maya: We often use a hybrid SLO: TTFT p95 for assistant routes, and TPOT p99 or total request p99 for heavy generation. The acceptance criteria can be weighted by traffic share so you don't overfit to rare heavy calls.
[02:00] James: How do you measure TPOT in the real world? Does Redwood measure per-token latencies server-side or do we need to sample network traces?
[02:08] Raj: We capture server-side token emission timestamps and client-received times for TTFT measurement. For TPOT we compute tokens/sec at the server and look at total per-request time, and we also bucket by sequence length. We can provide the benchmark harness that emits timestamps and aggregates p50/p95/p99.
[02:25] Samir: That sounds good. Our immediate risk is spikes during business hours causing 99th percentile slowness — we've had incidents where heavy batched requests from analytics flood the GPU and make interactive flows sluggish.
[02:36] Emma: Our control plane can route critical customers to isolation but we want to prove Redwood's autoscaling and fallback policies work under our mixed load.
[02:45] Maya: Okay so success criteria from Redwood's POV - we propose: TTFT p95 < 180ms for interactive routes, and TPOT p99 < X ms per token for generation routes (we'll calculate X once we see your token distribution). Additionally, no more than 2x cost per token vs your current baseline after quantization and caching.
[03:07] James: 180ms seems aggressive, but I guess feasible for smaller tokens. What's the current observed TTFT p95?
[03:13] Samir: Current is around 340ms at p95 during normal hours and spikes to 700ms at p99 during bursts.
[03:20] Raj: That delta indicates KV cache and batching opportunities. In our POC we can test both: baseline (no prefix cache) and optimized (prefix/KV cache + continuous batching) to show delta.
[03:30] Maya: For the POC timeline we propose 3 weeks: week 0 — prep and data exchange, week 1 — baseline runs and profiling, week 2 — optimization runs and validation, week 3 — final acceptance and handoff. Does that align?
[03:43] Emma: We were thinking 4 weeks but flexible if we get quick access to traces and infra.
[03:48] Maya: Great, we can expand if needed. Next — measurement plan specifics. Raj?
[03:53] Raj: We'll run two axis of experiments: one replay of anonymized production traces (replay harness) to get realistic input distribution, and one synthetic sweep to stress tail. For replay we need 3-7 days of traces, anonymized uids and tokens, split into sampling windows. We'll run at observed qps and also at 1.5x and 2x to test headroom. For synthetic we will generate high-length sequences to stress TPOT tails.
[04:21] Samir: About sampling windows — do you need full request bodies or just metadata?
[04:27] Raj: Ideally, for fidelity we need input length distribution and sequence prefixes. You can strip user text and replace with token counts; that's acceptable. We also need timestamps to reconstruct bursts.
[04:36] Samir: We can do that. We'll check privacy constraints with security.
[04:40] Maya: Good. On metrics, we'll capture TTFT, per-token emission latency, total latency per request, GPU utilization, queue lengths, batching stats, and per-route cost estimates. We'll also output the raw latency traces so you can compute p95/p99 yourselves.
[04:55] James: And for acceptance — you mentioned weighted SLOs? Explain that.
[04:58] Raj: Sure. A weighted SLO means you weight each route's SLO by its traffic share. For example 70% interactive with TTFT p95 < 180ms and 30% generation with TPOT p99 < X ms/token. The overall pass is if the weighted violation rate is below threshold, e.g., less than 1% of requests violating SLO. That avoids a single rare heavy job failing the whole pilot.
[05:22] Emma: That helps. Also, what about cold starts and model warmup effects? Our models sit in a model pool that sometimes gets swapped out.
[05:29] Raj: We'll simulate cold start events in the synthetic sweep and measure impact on both TTFT and TPOT. We can also demonstrate warmup policies to reduce cold start effect.
[05:36] Samir: One thing — can Redwood run in our VPC for this POC? We need to validate private deployment behavior.
[05:42] Maya: Yes, we offer a private VPC-attached deployment for POCs. For time-boxed benchmarks we can spin up a sandbox in your VPC or run in Redwood dedicated and mirror network characteristics. You should decide — VPC gives higher fidelity but requires infra onboarding.
[05:55] James: Onboarding time? We need estimate.
[05:57] Maya: For a minimal VPC test we usually need 3 business days for connection and credentials, up to a week if your security team requests CF templates and deep review.
[06:06] Samir: We're willing to go VPC if needed. Emma will check with security.
[06:09] Emma: Will do.
[06:11] Raj: A couple of notes about measurement noise — network jitter can affect TTFT seen by clients. We'll provide both server-side and end-to-end measurements. Server-side TTFT is the authoritative metric for SLOs but end-to-end is useful for UX.
[06:24] Samir: Good distinction. Also, cost model — can you estimate cost per 1M tokens for the optimized vs baseline?
[06:30] Maya: We can produce an estimated cost delta after the first baseline run; we typically show percentage reduction from batching, caching and quantization. We'll include a cost worksheet in the workbook.
[06:39] James: Ok. For SLO thresholds — can we tentatively set TTFT p95 to 220ms and TPOT p99 to 15ms/token for the pilot until you get our traces?
[06:49] Raj: That's reasonable as a starting hypothesis. We'll compute a more precise TPOT target after we sample the token length distribution.
[06:56] Samir: I'm noting that 15ms/token at p99 for long sequences could be expensive, so we'll watch cost tradeoffs.
[07:03] Maya: We'll also run a risk register: risks like data privacy delays, infra onboarding, cold-start variance, and measurement drift. We'll include mitigations and contingency windows.
[07:14] Samir: One more thing about the benchmarks — we prefer reproducibility. Can you provide the harness and docker image so our infra team can run it locally if needed?
[07:21] Raj: Absolutely, we'll share a containerized harness and a README. We'll also include a synthetic traffic generator and replay script.
[07:28] Emma: About logging and audit — we need audit logs for every request for compliance. Can Redwood surface that?
[07:33] Maya: Yes, we can provide audit logs and KMS key integration in private deployments. We'll share the SOC2/ISO docs as part of the security packet.
[07:41] James: Great. On timeline recap — you suggested a 3-week pilot, but we might extend to 4. Let's pick milestones: data handoff, baseline run, optimization run, and acceptance.
[07:52] Maya: Exactly. Milestone dates in action items. We'll sync with your calendar after this call.
[07:57] Samir: Sounds good. A few clarifying Qs — when you say p99, are you measuring across all tokens in a request or per-token emission p99?
[08:05] Raj: Both. We'll report per-token emission p99 and per-request total p99. For TPOT we often prefer per-token because it isolates emission speed independent of sequence length, but per-request p99 is what the product team cares about.
[08:17] Maya: Ok any blockers on your side for the data handoff?
[08:20] Emma: Security review might take a day or two. We need to confirm retention windows for traces.
[08:25] James: And we need to confirm whether we want VPC or dedicated sandbox. I'll discuss with infra and come back.
[08:31] Samir: Good.
[08:33] Maya: Great — last section quick walkthrough of the benchmark deliverables: baseline report with p50/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT, an optimization report with delta improvements, cost worksheet, and runbook for long-term ops. We'll also include a short demo video showing failure modes and fallback.
[08:51] Samir: Fantastic.
[08:53] Raj: Ok, I'll also include a sample SLO matrix in the workbook — weighted pass criteria, sampling windows, and tickets for follow-ups.
[09:02] Maya: Anything else?
[09:04] James: No, thank you.
[09:06] Emma: No, thanks.
[09:07] Samir: Thanks all.
[09:09] Maya: We'll send the workbook and the next steps now. Bye everyone.
[09:13] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: transcription has occasional mis-hearings — e.g., TPOT sometimes appears as "T P O T" in quick notes; proper nouns redwood/Velorum sometimes mis-capitalized.
